title: Grace and cooperation
hookLine: Catholics stress grace that heals and lifts, and our free cooperation with it

lines: YET NOT I, BUT THE GRACE OF GOD.
cards: Halfway through a sentence, Paul changes his mind about who did the work. Writing to the church in Corinth about his years on the road, he starts out sounding like a boast: "I laboured more abundantly than they all."
Then he catches himself, right there on the page: "yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me." So which is it? Did Paul work harder than the other apostles, or did grace do it?
He seems to say both, in one breath, and feels no need to choose. That little correction is a doorway into how Catholics talk about being saved.

teach.b: Grace is God's free gift of his own help and life. In Catholic teaching it always comes first. Nobody earns the start.
But grace doesn't push a person around like a chess piece. It heals the will and lifts it, so the person can freely say yes, and keep saying it.
That's cooperation: working together. Paul uses that very idea in his first letter to Corinth: "For we are labourers together with God." That's the shape of his correction: I worked hard, yet not I.
Not half and half, like two people splitting a bill.
More like a sail and the wind. The wind does the moving. The sail still has to be raised.
Catholic teaching points to Mary as a picture of this. An angel brings her an astonishing message, and she asks a real question: "How shall this be?"
Then she answers: "be it unto me according to thy word." Grace came to her first. Her yes was still her own.
Augustine, in a sermon, put it in a way tradition still repeats: the God who made you without you will not justify you without you.

Protestants, as we heard two days ago, stress that faith itself is a gift so no one can boast, and guard against anything that sounds like earning. Catholics answer that our yes is itself a fruit of grace.
Both are protecting the same thing: it all starts with God.

how: Catholics receive grace above all through the sacraments, such as baptism, confession and the Eucharist, and in the Angelus and the rosary they repeat Mary's words, be it done unto me according to thy word, as a pattern of saying yes to God.

grace comes first. it heals and lifts the will so the person can freely say yes.
Paul calls himself and his coworkers workers together with God
in 1 Corinthians 3:9 he says they work together with God.

games.q: you're Mary. an angel has just told you astonishing news. what do you do first?
o: say yes at once, without a word.
ask a real question: how shall this be?
refuse until you've had time to think.
games.why: she asks, "how shall this be?" then says, "be it unto me according to thy word." grace came first; her yes was still her own.

practice: Think of one gift you have and didn't make yourself: a steady hand, a good ear, a free hour this afternoon.
In this teaching, that's a place grace has already been at work, so picture one person who could use it, and one small, real step for them.
If you pray, offer that gift back to God and ask for help to use it; if you don't, just settle on the person and the step.

wordCard.voice: Grace and cooperation. God's gift comes first, healing and lifting the will, and the person freely works together with it.

orig.note: Greek: coworkers, those who work together. 1 Corinthians 3:9: working together with God.

carryVoice: Your line: grace and yes. The wind does the moving, and the sail still goes up. Same time tomorrow.
